An open-source coding model has been released that outperforms Claude Opus 4.7 on key benchmarks

DeepReinforce has released Ornith-1.0, a family of open-source models tailored for agent encoding. There are four variants: 9B Dense, 31B Dense, 35B MoE, and 397B MoE. Based on Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.5.

The key idea of the model is that it learns not only to solve tasks but also to build scenarios for their solutions. Conventional models receive a ready-made "framework" of how to approach the task and work with it. Ornith generates and improves it during the training process.

The flagship 397B version scored 77.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 82.4 on SWE-Bench Verified. Claude Opus 4.7 on the same tests shows 70.3 and 80.8.

The 35B version outperforms Qwen 3.5-397B on Terminal-Bench, meaning a model eleven times smaller in parameters works better on this test.

The 9B variant, which runs on regular hardware, outperforms Gemma 4-31B on several benchmarks.

All models are available on Hugging Face.

Binance has warned its European users that it will stop providing crypto services in the EU after failing to secure a MiCA license before the deadline

On June 24, the exchange withdrew its license application in Greece and announced plans to apply in another EU country. However, with MiCA rules fully taking effect on July 1, time has run out. 

In emails sent to users, Binance's European entity stated that it can no longer accept new clients and will cease providing crypto-asset services from July 1, 2026.

Users in Poland, Italy, Spain, and France have already received instructions on how to withdraw their funds. 

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao criticized the decision, saying it's "sad to see the European Union deprive its users of access to the best liquidity in the world."

For now, this looks like a major setback for Binance in Europe and another reminder that regulation is becoming one of the biggest challenges for global crypto exchanges.

A guide to Loop Engineering has been released — a new approach to working with AI agents

The repository loop-engineering has been published, offering a paradigm shift: instead of manually prompting AI agents, the developer designs a cycle that does this automatically. 🔄🤖

The author notes that most people still use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Grok as a regular chat: prompt → wait → copy → correct → prompt again. Loop Engineering proposes to stop being a "nanny" for the agent and instead build a system where agents work, check, correct, and escalate on their own. 🛠️⚙️

The repository includes ready-made cycles for daily triage, PR, CI, dependencies, changelog, and issues. It includes CLI for creating cycles, evaluating tokens, auditing the repository, and safely running agents via GitHub Actions. 📋✅

"Prompt engineering was about how to write better prompts. Loop engineering is about creating a system where agents continue to work without your supervision at every step," the description says. 🚀🧠

The repository is available on GitHub.

Occupation by Invitation

Israel's Lebanon deal isn't a peace treaty; it's a legal rebranding of occupation with a nice press release and a very shaky fuse.
On paper, the IDF stays on "almost all" the territory it seized until Hezbollah is disarmed and its infrastructure "destroyed across Lebanon." 

That's not a benchmark; it's a blank check. You can call it "by invitation of the sovereign Lebanese state," but it converts a de facto occupation into a de jure "presence with permission," signed under massive military pressure — and the fact that Hezbollah ministers sit in the cabinet that signed it doesn't make it cleaner. It just folds the Lebanese state's fragmentation into Israel's legal shield.

The claim that "no one can now demand Israel withdraw" is wishful thinking dressed as lawfare. Iran, Turkey, France, the UN, the Arab states will still call it occupation if the IDF stays for years. The paper doesn't neutralize politics; it just hands Jerusalem a talking point in Brussels and Washington: "We're not occupiers, we're guests." 

That's why the EU rushed to bless the deal as a "critical step away from escalation" while cutting a modest refugee check — it lets everyone pretend something changed without forcing Israel to leave.
This isn't recognition; it's coercion. 

Beirut signed because it has no military alternative and hopes the army's deployment limits the next round of destruction. But for much of the public — not just Hezbollah's base — it reads as an enemy army left on their land. 

That's not durable legitimacy; it's a recipe for another round of "resistance," under Hezbollah's brand or a successor's.
The "pilot" withdrawals are a test balloon, and the asymmetry is baked in: Israel alone decides when the pilot has "failed," while Lebanon's only leverage is to threaten the one thing no one wants — renewed fighting. 

Meanwhile Lebanon is asked to holster its few non-military tools, from ICC filings to Western lobbying, in exchange for fewer airstrikes.
The biggest hole is domestic Israeli politics. 

The deal assumes the same leadership that walked into a two-front war will now manage a disciplined, low-profile "presence by invitation" — no overreach, no mission creep, no future government deciding to "adjust the lines" in ways that blow up the framework. 

It assumes a rationality recent history doesn't support.
So from a narrow legal-bureaucratic angle, it's a win: more legitimacy, more time, almost no withdrawal. 

From any wider perspective it's a frozen conflict with a nicer wrapper — a state-sanctioned occupation that keeps generating grievances for everyone who thrives on "resistance." 

If that's "a great success," it's the kind you only call great because all the other options are worse.
